item.title: Population-Based Evaluation of a Multidimensional Diagnostic Schema for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
item.dc:creator: Jonas Eriksson Ström
Ida Pesonen
Joel Bergqvist
Gabriella Eliason
Hannes Holm Isholth
Petra Kristina Jacobson
Emily Krantz
Marina Labor
item.description:
Authors: Jonas Eriksson Ström, Ida Pesonen, Joel Bergqvist, Gabriella Eliason, Hannes Holm Isholth, Petra Kristina Jacobson, Emily Krantz, Marina Labor, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance A multidimensional chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) diagnostic schema incorporating imaging and clinical features beyond airflow obstruction has been proposed. However, its implications for prevalence, case composition, and prognostic stratification in the general population remain unknown. Objective To compare the population-level classification and prognostic implications of a multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema with those of the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) definition. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based cohort study used the Swedish Cardiopulmonary Bioimage Study, conducted at 6 Swedish university hospitals 2013-2018 to compare diagnostic definitions in the full cohort and in a symptom-restricted subgroup approximating routine clinical practice, with mortality follow-up through September 30, 2024. Randomly sampled adults aged 50 to 64 years with complete classification data, including postbronchodilator spirometry and chest computed tomography assessment of emphysema and bronchial wall thickening were included. Exposure Classification according to the multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema and an operationalized GOLD definition. Main Outcomes and Measures COPD prevalence, case composition, and all-cause mortality. Results A total of 29 281 participants (15011 females [51.3%]; mean [SD] age, 57.5 [4.3] years) were included; 1347 participants (4.6%) met multidimensional COPD criteria. In analyses restricted to 6016 symptomatic individuals, prevalence was similar under the multidimensional and GOLD definitions (909 [15.1%] vs 853 [14.2%]), but case composition differed. Approximately one-third of patients with multidimensional COPD (281 of 909 [30.9%]) did not meet the GOLD criteria. Across the full cohort, 438 individuals (32.5% of multidimensional COPD cases) were asymptomatic and would be unlikely to undergo diagnostic evaluation in routine symptom-driven care. During follow-up, 634 deaths occurred. Among symptomatic participants, adjusted mortality risk was increased in multidimensional-only cases (hazard ratio [HR], 2.58; 95% CI, 1.66-4.01) and those meeting both definitions (HR, 2.20; 95% CI, 1.59-3.04), but not in patients with GOLD-only COPD (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.44-2.00). Conclusions and Relevance In this population-based cohort study, COPD prevalence was similar with a multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema to that obtained using GOLD criteria, but case composition differed substantially. The multidimensional schema identified increased mortality risk among individuals not captured by GOLD, suggesting improved prognostic stratification, while the identification of many asymptomatic cases highlights an existing detection gap in current symptom-driven care pathways.

item.title: Removing Race From Standardized Mortality Ratio Risk Adjustment in Dialysis Care Quality Measurement
item.dc:creator: Kalli G. Koukounas
Louis Boyang
Christopher H. Schmid
Rachel E. Patzer
Adam S. Wilk
Kelsey M. Drewry
Rajnish Mehrotra
Maricruz Rivera-Hernandez
item.description:
Authors: Kalli G. Koukounas, Louis Boyang, Christopher H. Schmid, Rachel E. Patzer, Adam S. Wilk, Kelsey M. Drewry, Rajnish Mehrotra, Maricruz Rivera-Hernandez, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) adjusts for race and ethnicity when calculating and publicly reporting standardized mortality ratios (SMRs) of dialysis facilities. In July 2025, CMS removed race, ethnicity, and related demographic fields from the End-Stage Renal Disease Medical Evidence Report—the primary data source for race and ethnicity in SMR risk adjustment. Objective To evaluate how removing race and ethnicity from SMR calculations is associated with facility-level performance, particularly among facilities serving high proportions of patients with social risk factors. Design, Setting, and Participants In this cross-sectional study using the US Renal Data and Renal Management Information Systems, data from dialysis facilities in the US during the period of January 2017 to December 2020 were analyzed from October 2025 to January 2026. Facilities were categorized into quintiles based on the proportion of incident patients who were non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, living in highly disadvantaged neighborhoods, or uninsured or Medicaid-covered at dialysis initiation. A composite social risk score classified facilities as being in the highest quintile of none, 1, or at least 2 of these characteristics. Exposure Race and ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and insurance coverage proportions of patients. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes were change in facility-level SMR values and rankings after the removal of race and ethnicity from risk adjustment. Results Among 6895 dialysis facilities, 6220 (90.2%) were for profit, and 1588 (23.0%) had the highest social risk score of 2 or higher. With race-inclusive adjustment, the mean (SD) SMR among facilities with the lowest social risk was 0.93 (0.39), compared with 1.03 (0.42) among facilities with the highest social risk (difference, 0.10; 95% CI, 0.09-0.12). After removing race and ethnicity, this difference was nearly eliminated to −0.002 (95% CI, −0.02 to 0.01). A total of 1259 facilities (21.6%) with high social risk improved in SMR ranking after race exclusion, compared with 236 facilities (1.9%) with low social risk (difference, 19.7; 95% CI, 18.4-20.9 percentage points). Facilities serving the highest proportion of non-Hispanic Black patients experienced the greatest gains, with 26.6% improving SMR performance, compared with 4.7% among all other facilities (difference, 21.9; 95% CI, 20.5-23.3 percentage points). Conclusions and Relevance Results of this cross-sectional study suggest that removing race and ethnicity from SMR risk adjustment substantially altered publicly reported mortality performance among dialysis facilities, with the largest changes among facilities serving larger proportions of Black patients. These findings suggest that excluding race and ethnicity from SMR risk adjustment may meaningfully shift performance comparisons in favor of facilities serving populations with greater social risk.

item.title: Reducing Low-Value Care Through the Smarter Care Virginia Initiative
item.dc:creator: John N. Mafi
Beth A. Bortz
Sitaram Vangala
Chi-Hong Tseng
Kyle Russell
Manying Cui
Artem Romanov
Howard Beckman
item.description:
Authors: John N. Mafi, Beth A. Bortz, Sitaram Vangala, Chi-Hong Tseng, Kyle Russell, Manying Cui, Artem Romanov, Howard Beckman, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Low-value care costs more than $100 billion annually and remains pervasive despite decades of evidence documenting its clinical and financial harms. While several US states have begun discouraging its use, the feasibility of such statewide interventions in partnership with large health systems remains unknown. Objective To investigate the effectiveness of a clinician-led, multistakeholder, statewide initiative to reduce low-value care in the Commonwealth of Virginia. Design, Setting, and Participants This quality improvement study used a difference-in-differences analyses comparing low-value service changes among patients attributed to 6 health systems vs 12 control systems in the Commonwealth of Virginia preintervention (January 1 to December 31, 2019) vs postintervention (January 1 to December 31, 2022). Any patient eligible to receive 1 or more of the 9 measured low-value services in the 18 health systems evaluated were included. Data were analyzed between December 1, 2023, and September 1, 2026. Exposure The intervention, Smarter Care Virginia, included health system financial support, clinician education, and quarterly peer-comparison performance scorecards. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the percentage of patients receiving any of 9 selected low-value services: (1-3) preoperative laboratory, imaging, and cardiac testing; (4-5) electrocardiogram/cardiac screening and cardiac stress testing; (6-7) diagnostic imaging and opioids for acute back pain; (8) advanced diagnostic eye imaging; and (9) peripherally inserted central catheter lines for patients with chronic kidney disease. Secondary outcomes included adverse events (eg, myocardial infarction–related hospitalization) and per-capita spending on the 9 low-value services. Results A total of 17 223 clinicians (7222 in the intervention group and 10 001 in the control group) and 4.5 million patients (approximately 68% of Virginia’s adult population) were identified. In 2019, 10.5% of patients in the intervention group and 10.7% of patients in the control group received 1 or more low-value services; in 2021 to 2022, rates declined to 8.5% and 9.1%, respectively. The intervention was associated with 10.4% fewer patients receiving 1 or more low-value services (absolute reduction, −1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, −2.1 to −0.1 percentage points; P = .04). There was no statistically significant change in adverse events (0.03%; 95% CI, −0.02% to 0.03%; P = .84) or spending on the 9 low-value services ($0.33; 95% CI, −$3.43 to $4.11). Conclusions and Relevance In this quality improvement study, a statewide, clinician-led initiative was associated with a small but statistically significant reduction in low-value care delivery without evidence of harm. Achieving larger reductions may require combining such health system–driven efforts with additional strategies, such as payment reform and physician and hospital accountability, that discourage the use of low-value care.

item.title: Drug Burden Index Stewardship to Deprescribe Anticholinergic or Sedative Drugs in Older Inpatients
item.dc:creator: Kenji Fujita
Nashwa Masnoon
Danijela Gnjidic
Christopher Etherton-Beer
Emily Reeve
Parker Magin
J. Simon Bell
Kenneth Rockwood
item.description:
Authors: Kenji Fujita, Nashwa Masnoon, Danijela Gnjidic, Christopher Etherton-Beer, Emily Reeve, Parker Magin, J. Simon Bell, Kenneth Rockwood, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Anticholinergic and sedative medications contribute to poor clinical outcomes in older inpatients. Evidence-based deprescribing strategies are needed. Objective To evaluate whether an intervention bundle increases deprescribing of anticholinergic and sedative medications in older inpatients. Design, Setting, and Participants This stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 6 Australian public hospitals from January 2022 to July 2023. Participants were patients 65 years and older with Drug Burden Index (DBI; a measure of anticholinergic and sedative medication exposure) score greater than 0 at admission and hospitalized for 48 hours or more. Data were analyzed from October 2023 to May 2026. Interventions The intervention bundle had 2 components. The informational component (automated DBI score calculation displayed in the electronic medical record, deprescribing guides, patient leaflets, and education module) was present in all trial phases, although clinicians were not informed of it during the control phase. The stewardship component (study stewardship pharmacists who promoted the informational component and made patient-level deprescribing recommendations to attending teams) was delivered in the intervention phase. The informational component was promoted 1 to 2 times monthly during the sustainability phase. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with 1 or more DBI-contributing medications deprescribed (ceased or dose reduced) at discharge compared with admission. Secondary outcomes included deprescribing recommendations in discharge summaries and in-hospital adverse events. Results Among 4827 included patients, 2798 (58.0%) were female, and the median (IQR) age was 83.0 (76.0-88.0) years. The proportion of patients with 1 or more DBI-contributing medications deprescribed was 38.1% (788 of 2069) in the control phase, 41.4% (326 of 788) in the intervention phase, and 37.0% (729 of 1970) in the sustainability phase. The adjusted absolute difference (aAD) between intervention and control was 5.3 percentage points (95% CI, 0.1-10.6), smaller than hypothesized. Deprescribing was predominantly by cessation; in the intervention phase, 256 of 788 patients (32.5%) had 1 or more DBI-contributing medications ceased, 91 (11.5%) had 1 or more doses reduced, and 21 (2.7%) had both. The aAD between the sustainability and intervention phase estimates was −5.3 percentage points (95% CI, −10.9 to 0.3). Deprescribing recommendations in discharge summaries were more prevalent in the intervention (176 of 751 admissions [23.4%]) than the control phase (287 of 1968 admissions [14.6%]; aAD, 10.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.0-15.1) and were lower in the sustainability phase (362 of 1910 [19.0%]; aAD, −4.0 percentage points; 95% CI, −8.7 to 0.8). In-hospital adverse events were similar across phases. Conclusions and Relevance In this stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial, the intervention bundle increased deprescribing less than hypothesized, and the increase was not sustained once the stewardship component ended. Trial Registration Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12622000374763

item.title: Risk of Shoulder Injury Related to Vaccine Administration for COVID-19 and Influenza Vaccinations
item.dc:creator: Chengyi Zheng
Lei Qian
Lina S. Sy
Gabriella V. Goodwin
Meiyu Yeh
Ronald A. Navarro
Dawn T. Asamura
Denison S. Ryan
item.description:
Authors: Chengyi Zheng, Lei Qian, Lina S. Sy, Gabriella V. Goodwin, Meiyu Yeh, Ronald A. Navarro, Dawn T. Asamura, Denison S. Ryan, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine identified a critical evidence gap regarding the risk of shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA) after COVID-19 vaccination. Objective To compare the risk of SIRVA after COVID-19 vs influenza vaccinations in adults. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based cohort study included individuals aged at least 18 years who received a COVID-19 or influenza vaccination administered via intramuscular deltoid injection between August 1, 2023, and April 30, 2024, at Kaiser Permanente Southern California. Data were analyzed from June 2024 to September 2026. Exposure Receipt of COVID-19 vaccination or influenza vaccination. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was incident SIRVA, defined as shoulder symptoms beginning at or before 7 days and persisting more than 30 days after vaccination, identified using a validated natural language processing algorithm. Incidences were calculated per 10 000 vaccinations. Adjusted relative risks (RRs), risk differences, and 95% CIs were estimated using robust Poisson regression with inverse probability of treatment weighting. Results A total of 1 366 362 individuals (mean [SD] age at vaccination, 58.4 [18.2] years; 782 994 female [57.3%]) across 1 901 588 vaccinations were included (1 076 609 vaccinations [56.7%] were administered to females). Among 1 830 636 vaccinations in the primary analysis, 252 SIRVA cases were identified as follows: 110 cases (0.018%) after 596 614 COVID-19 vaccinations and 142 cases (0.012%) after 1 234 022 influenza vaccinations. An additional 13 SIRVA cases (0.018%) were identified among 70 952 simultaneous COVID-19 and influenza vaccinations. Most COVID-19 vaccines were Pfizer-BioNTech messenger RNA (667 455 of 667 566 [99.98%]), and influenza vaccines were predominantly standard-dose (866 530 of 1 304 974 [66.40%]) or high-dose (438 183 of 1 304 974 [33.58%]) inactivated quadrivalent formulations. SIRVA incidence was higher after COVID-19 than influenza vaccination, at an incidence of 1.84 (95% CI, 1.53-2.22) vs 1.15 (95% CI, 0.98-1.36) per 10 000 vaccinations, corresponding to an adjusted absolute increase of 0.67 cases (95% CI, 0.15-1.19) per 10 000 vaccinations (adjusted RR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.16-2.28). Among adults 65 years or older, SIRVA incidence was 2.11 (95% CI, 1.67-2.67) per 10 000 for COVID-19 vaccination and 1.63 (95% CI, 1.28-2.07) per 10 000 for high-dose influenza vaccination (adjusted RR, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.92-2.15). Conclusions and Relevance Results of this cohort study suggest that although SIRVA was rarely associated with both vaccines, COVID-19 vaccination was associated with approximately 7 additional cases per 100 000 vaccinations compared with influenza vaccination. Among adults aged 65 years or older, SIRVA risk did not differ significantly between COVID-19 and high-dose influenza vaccination. The small absolute risk of SIRVA should be considered alongside the established benefits of COVID-19 and influenza vaccination in preventing severe disease and hospitalization.

item.title: Surveillance Mammography and Second Primary Breast Cancer Diagnosis Among Older Women With a History of Breast Cancer
item.dc:creator: Ilana B. Richman
Jessica B. Long
Meghan E. Lindsay
Meera Sheffrin
Elizabeth R. Berger
item.description:
Authors: Ilana B. Richman, Jessica B. Long, Meghan E. Lindsay, Meera Sheffrin, Elizabeth R. Berger
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Although surveillance mammography is commonly performed among older women, whether this practice improves clinical outcomes in this population is uncertain. Objective To evaluate the association between surveillance mammography and second primary breast cancer stage at diagnosis among older women with a history of breast cancer. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective longitudinal cohort study used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program–Medicare data. Women with nonmetastatic breast cancer that was diagnosed from 2004 to 2008 at 67 years or older who had a surveillance mammogram at approximately 5 years after diagnosis were included. Analyses used cause-specific hazard models with inverse probability of treatment weighting to estimate the risk of stage-specific second primary breast cancer among women who continued surveillance mammography and those who did not. Analyses were stratified by hormone receptor (HR) status of the initial breast cancer. Follow-up continued until second breast cancer diagnosis, death, or end of the study (December 2021). Analyses were performed between November 2025 and August 2026. Exposure Continued surveillance mammography more than 5 years after initial diagnosis. Main Outcomes and Measures Stage-specific cumulative incidence of a second primary breast cancer, categorized as in situ, localized, or advanced (regional or distant). Results Among 9888 women (mean [SD] age, 81.1 [5.5] years; 387 Hispanic [3.9%], 514 non-Hispanic Black [5.1%], and 8514 White individuals [86.1%]), 8055 (81.4%) had in situ or localized disease and 7621 (76.9%) had HR-positive tumors at initial diagnosis. Overall, 7940 women (80.3%) continued surveillance at cohort entry. Advanced second primary breast cancer was rare, and incidence did not differ among those who continued surveillance and those who did not (cumulative incidence, 1.65% vs 2.15%; hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.46-1.26). Results were similar in subgroups of women with initial HR-positive and HR-negative breast cancer. Conclusions and Relevance The results of this cohort study suggest that among older survivors of breast cancer, continued surveillance mammography was not associated with a reduced risk of advanced second primary breast cancer. The absolute risk of advanced cancer was low, and surveillance decisions should be individualized given the potential burdens of continued surveillance.

item.title: Timing of Initiation of Methadone Take-Home Dosing
item.dc:creator: Md. Belal Hossain
Jeong Eun Min
Megan Kurz
Shaun Seaman
Paxton Bach
Mohammad Ehsanul Karim
Julie Bruneau
Maria Eugenia Socias
item.description:
Authors: Md. Belal Hossain, Jeong Eun Min, Megan Kurz, Shaun Seaman, Paxton Bach, Mohammad Ehsanul Karim, Julie Bruneau, Maria Eugenia Socias, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine; Volume: 186; Issue: 11; Pages: 1347
Abstract: Importance Daily witnessed ingestion in community-based pharmacies is standard practice for methadone maintenance treatment for opioid use disorder in British Columbia, Canada. Whether this practice, compared with take-home methadone, may pose a barrier to sustained retention in treatment and its lifesaving benefits is not known. Objective To assess the different initiation times of methadone take-home doses in terms of time to all-cause mortality and methadone discontinuation, defined as a gap in prescribed doses lasting 5 or more days. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study using principles of target trial emulation used observational data from British Columbia, Canada, 2010-2022. Both incident (no history of opioid agonist treatment [OAT]) and prevalent new-user (no OAT within the past month) designs were used. The study included individuals aged 18 years or older who completed OAT induction, were not pregnant or incarcerated, and had no history of cancer treatment or palliative care. Data analyses were conducted from March 5, 2025, to May 29, 2026. Exposure Exposure strategies were (1) no take-home dosing, (2) take-home dose initiation within 0 to 4 weeks after completing induction, (3) take-home dose initiation within 5 to 12 weeks after completing induction, (4) take-home dose initiation within 13 to 24 weeks after completing induction, and (5) take-home dose initiation within 25 to 52 weeks after completing induction. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes were time to all-cause mortality and methadone discontinuation. A clone-censor-weight approach was used to estimate the 78-week adjusted risk difference (ARD). Results A total of 9788 incident users (median age, 34.1 [IQR, 27.2-44.1] years; 32.8% female) and 31 658 prevalent new users (median age, 36.9 [IQR, 29.7-46.2] years; 33.3% female) were included. Compared with no take-home dosing in prevalent new-user analysis, ARDs for the mortality outcome were −0.87 (95% CI, −1.51 to −0.23) for take-home dose initiation within 0 to 4 weeks after completing induction, −0.98 (95% CI, −1.62 to −0.33) for take-home dose initiation within 5 to 12 weeks after completing induction, −0.82 (95% CI, −1.59 to −0.06) for take-home dose initiation within 13 to 24 weeks after completing induction, and −0.31 (95% CI, −1.05 to 0.44) for take-home dose initiation within 25 to 52 weeks after completing induction. Compared with no take-home dosing in prevalent new-user analysis, the discontinuation outcome ARDs were −2.04 (95% CI, −3.99 to −0.10) for take-home dose initiation within 0 to 4 weeks after completing induction, −5.29 (95% CI, −6.82 to −3.76) for take-home dose initiation within 5 to 12 weeks after completing induction, −5.97 (95% CI, −7.16 to −4.78) for take-home dose initiation within 13 to 24 weeks after completing induction, and −4.39 (95% CI, −5.37 to −3.42) for take-home dose initiation within 25 to 52 weeks after completing induction. Similar patterns were observed among incident users. Multiple sensitivity analyses with sample restrictions, time-0 classifications, timeline restrictions, and addressing residual confounding bias supported the primary results. Conclusions and Relevance Results of this study suggest that initiating take-home methadone within 5 to 12 weeks and 13 to 24 weeks after completing induction resulted in the greatest benefits in reducing mortality and treatment discontinuation, although any take-home dosing was consistently better than no take-home dosing. These client-level benefits warrant consideration when refining clinical guidelines on take-home dosing.

item.dc:creator: Ryan E. Wiegand
Heng-Ming Sung
Yue Zhang
Andrea J. Chavez
Kelly M. Hatfield
Amber Kautz
Josephine Mak
Morgan Najdowski
item.description:
Authors: Ryan E. Wiegand, Heng-Ming Sung, Yue Zhang, Andrea J. Chavez, Kelly M. Hatfield, Amber Kautz, Josephine Mak, Morgan Najdowski, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine; Volume: 186; Issue: 11; Pages: 1335
Abstract: Importance Vaccine effectiveness (VE) estimates are needed to determine the effectiveness of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccinations during their first season of availability among populations at high risk for severe RSV. Objective To assess RSV VE against RSV-associated outcomes for nursing home residents. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study of Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries used electronic medical claims data from September 10, 2023, to March 30, 2024. A cohort was created for each outcome: an RSV-associated hospitalization cohort; an RSV-associated death cohort; a severe RSV-associated outcome cohort; and an RSV-associated thromboembolic event cohort. To be eligible for inclusion in a cohort, a Medicare fee-for-service beneficiary must be aged 65 years or older, reside in a US nursing home during the study period for at least 1 day, have continuous enrollment in Medicare Parts A and B (365 days prior to the index date), and have continuous enrollment in Part D (beginning on June 21, 2023). Exposure RSV vaccination. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes were RSV-associated hospitalization, RSV-associated death, severe RSV-associated outcomes (intensive care unit or critical care unit admission, medical ventilator use, or RSV-associated death), and RSV-associated thromboembolic event. RSV diagnoses and outcome definitions were based on claims with relevant International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision codes. RSV vaccine doses were determined from Medicare Part D claims using the National Drug Code Directory. Hazard ratios (HRs) from multivariable Cox proportional hazards models compared the times to first outcomes among RSV vaccinated beneficiaries and unvaccinated beneficiaries. VE was calculated as (1–HR) × 100%. Results Of 597 430 included Medicare beneficiaries (66% female; median age, 82 [IQR, 75-88] years), RSV VE against RSV-associated hospitalizations was 73% (95% CI, 65%-79%). Among beneficiaries aged 65 to 74 years VE was 60% (95% CI, 35%-76%), 75% (95% CI, 67%-82%) among beneficiaries 75 years or older, 67% (95% CI, 55%-76%) among short-stay residents (&amp;lt;100 cumulative days), and 80% (95% CI, 68%-87%) among long-stay residents (≥100 cumulative days). VE against RSV-associated death was 56% (95% CI, 39%-69%), VE against severe RSV-associated outcomes was 59% (95% CI, 44%-70%), and VE against RSV-associated thromboembolic events was 66% (95% CI, 44%-79%). Conclusions and Relevance In this study, in the first season of availability, RSV vaccines were associated with improved RSV-associated outcomes among US Medicare beneficiaries residing in nursing homes.

item.title: Menopausal Hormone Therapy and Cardiovascular Risk in Midlife Women With Vasomotor Symptoms
item.dc:creator: Ziyuan Wang
Sonja A. Swanson
Maria M. Brooks
Emma Barinas-Mitchell
Marnie Bertolet
Jared W. Magnani
Rebecca C. Thurston
Samar R. El Khoudary
item.description:
Authors: Ziyuan Wang, Sonja A. Swanson, Maria M. Brooks, Emma Barinas-Mitchell, Marnie Bertolet, Jared W. Magnani, Rebecca C. Thurston, Samar R. El Khoudary
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine; Volume: 186; Issue: 11; Pages: 1323
Abstract: Importance Vasomotor symptoms in perimenopause are associated with increased future cardiovascular (CVD) risk. Most clinical trials on menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) and CVD risk have focused on postmenopausal women, with limited study of the perimenopausal period when hormonal fluctuations and symptoms are greatest. Moreover, these trials were not designed to evaluate CVD risk with MHT among women with vasomotor symptoms. Objective To estimate the effect of MHT on CVD risk among perimenopausal and recently postmenopausal women with vasomotor symptoms and assess the extent to which timing of MHT use relative to menopause and race and ethnicity modify this effect. Design, Setting, and Participants Cohort data from the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation (SWAN, 1997-2017)—a multiethnic, multicenter, longitudinal study of the menopause transition—were used to emulate a sequence of target trials. Eligible participants were women who self-reported any vasomotor symptoms (ie, hot flashes and/or night sweats over the past 2 weeks) and who were CVD-free, with no prior MHT use. Data were analyzed from January 2023 to December 2025. Exposure MHT use (systemic estrogen with/without progestogens, verified from medication containers). Main Outcomes and Measures CVD events (myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, and revascularization) were self-reported. CVD-related death was recorded from death certificates. Results Of 2737 women who reported any vasomotor symptoms, 755 initiated MHT (mean [SD] age, 53.7 [4.6] years) over the 20-year follow-up period, during which 224 fatal and nonfatal CVD events occurred. Overall, the estimated adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) of CVD events for MHT initiation vs noninitiation was 0.78 (95% CI, 0.62-0.98). The estimated aHR was 0.73 (95% CI, 0.58-0.93) and 1.53 (95% CI, 0.66-3.52) among women initiating MHT 10 or fewer years vs more than 10 years from the onset of menopause, respectively ( P value for interaction: .02). Race and ethnicity modified the MHT initiation effect, with Black women showing protective effect (aHR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.33-0.81), while no clear effects were observed in White women or women of other races ( P value for interaction = .007). Conclusions and Relevance The presented results are pooled from all target trials and found that MHT initiation during perimenopause or recently postmenopausal women with vasomotor symptoms was estimated to reduce CVD risk by 22%. Benefits were more pronounced in Black women and women who initiated MHT within 10 years of menopause onset. However, all estimates warrant caution given the potential for residual confounding. Given the inconsistency of the cardiovascular benefits and the need to consider overall risk-benefit balance, these findings should not be used to support MHT for CVD prevention.

item.title: Telehealth Treatment of Anxiety in Patients With Low-Risk Chest Pain in the Emergency Department
item.dc:creator: Paul I. Musey
Kurt Kroenke
Jill Nault Connors
Timothy E. Stump
Yelena Chernyak
Kevin Prather
Chet Montgomery
Patrick O. Monahan
item.description:
Authors: Paul I. Musey, Kurt Kroenke, Jill Nault Connors, Timothy E. Stump, Yelena Chernyak, Kevin Prather, Chet Montgomery, Patrick O. Monahan
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine; Volume: 186; Issue: 11; Pages: 1300
Abstract: Importance Chest pain is a leading reason for emergency department (ED) visits, with most cases classified as low-risk chest pain (LRCP) after excluding acute coronary syndrome. Many patients with LRCP experience undiagnosed or undertreated anxiety. Objective To determine if 2 types of telehealth-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) interventions were superior to primary care referral for patients with LRCP and anxiety. Design, Setting, and Participants The Patient-Centered Treatment of Anxiety After Low-Risk Chest Pain in the Emergency Room (PACER) trial was a randomized, 3-group comparative effectiveness trial conducted across 6 university health systems EDs that enrolled adults with LRCP who were discharged from the ED and had at least moderate anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder–7 [GAD-7] score ≥8 or Patient Health Questionnaire [PHQ] panic screener score ≥2) from April 2021 to July 2024 (12-month follow-up was completed by July 2025). Data analysis began in July 2025 and was completed by January 2026. Interventions All 3 groups received psychoeducation. The 3 interventions compared were (1) recommended primary care follow-up, (2) peer-supported internet-based CBT (iCBT), and (3) therapist-delivered CBT via telehealth. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was change over 12 months in the GAD-7 anxiety score. Secondary outcomes included global anxiety improvement, PHQ-8 depression scores, PHQ-14 somatization scores, and Sheehan Disability Scale scores. Outcomes were assessed at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. Results A total of 375 patients were enrolled (265 female individuals [70.7%] and 109 male individuals [29.1%]; 125 Black individuals [33.3%], 28 Hispanic individuals [7.5%], 226 White individuals [60.3%], and 22 individuals [5.9%] of other race; mean [SD] age, 39.9 [13.1] years). Adjusted mean improvement in GAD-7 over 12 months was significant within all arms (4.32, 5.54, and 5.13 points in the primary care referral, peer-supported iCBT, and therapist-delivered CBT groups, respectively, for which the baseline SD pooled over groups that was used to calculate all effect sizes was 4.83). Improvement with peer-supported iCBT was 1.22 points greater (95% CI, 0.01-2.43; effect size = 0.25) than primary care referral, and this effect was strongest (2.8 points) among patients with severe anxiety. Depression, somatization, and disability improved moderately within groups, with no significant between-group differences. Odds of patient-reported global anxiety improvement were 3 times higher in the 2 CBT groups compared with primary care referral. Higher engagement was associated with greater anxiety reduction. Therapeutic alliance and program satisfaction were high in both CBT groups. Conclusions and Relevance The results of this randomized clinical trial suggest that peer-supported iCBT significantly reduces anxiety in ED patients with LRCP and elevated anxiety, with the greatest improvement occurring in patients with severe anxiety. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04811521

item.title: Effective Palliative Care for Hospice Transitions
item.dc:creator: May Hua
Miguel Cid
Claire Barshied
Rachel C. Shelton
Grace Hu
Natasha Stekl
Carrie Brill
Elise C. Carey
item.description:
Authors: May Hua, Miguel Cid, Claire Barshied, Rachel C. Shelton, Grace Hu, Natasha Stekl, Carrie Brill, Elise C. Carey, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine; Volume: 186; Issue: 11; Pages: 1369
Abstract: Importance Variation in hospice use for patients with cancer exists between palliative care programs, but factors underlying this heterogeneity are unknown. Objective To identify hospital and palliative care program factors that may impact the ability of palliative care teams to affect hospice use in cancer. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter qualitative study included 6 palliative care programs in the United States. Using a cohort of patients with metastatic cancer who received specialist palliative care, a positive-negative deviance approach was used to select 3 programs with high and 3 programs with low performance on hospice use. In-depth site visits were conducted and included semistructured interviews with palliative care and oncology clinicians and patients as well as in-person observation. Interviews were conducted from February 2025 to January 2026. Site visits were conducted from May 2025 to January 2026. Main Outcomes and Measures Program-specific practices and their potential effect on hospice use for patients with cancer. Results A total of 93 interviews and 424 hours of in-person observation were conducted across 6 palliative care programs in the Midwest, Upper South, and Deep South regions of the United States. Interview participants had a median (IQR) age of 43 (37-47) years; 68 (73.1%) were female; clinicians had a median (IQR) of 11 (5-16) years of experience. There were notable differences in the relationships between palliative care and oncology teams between high- and low-performing programs. At high-performing programs, the relationship was characterized by mutual trust and respect, warmth and familiarity, and empathy for each other, whereas at low-performing programs, the relationship was characterized by a lack of trust and familiarity and negative regard for each other. Factors observed in programs with positive relationships included intentionality in relationship building, physical presence and proximity between teams, use of real-time communication, and the palliative care team having a service-oriented mentality and a reputation for reliable service. At high-performing programs, observable differences in care included collaborative care delivery, increased access and timeliness of palliative care, and earlier introduction of hospice by oncology clinicians. Conclusions and Relevance In this multicenter qualitative study, differences in the relationship between palliative care and oncology teams were identified that may mechanistically affect end-of-life patient outcomes. These findings are important to ensure the delivery of high-quality care for all patients with cancer.

item.title: Fasting Duration and Differences Across Routine Laboratory Tests
item.dc:creator: Sunghwan Shin
Sollip Kim
Shinae Yu
Soo Jin Yoo
Kuenyoul Park
Jeonghyun Chang
Tae-Hyun Um
Chong Rae Cho
item.description:
Authors: Sunghwan Shin, Sollip Kim, Shinae Yu, Soo Jin Yoo, Kuenyoul Park, Jeonghyun Chang, Tae-Hyun Um, Chong Rae Cho, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine; Volume: 186; Issue: 11; Pages: 1312
Abstract: Importance Fasting before blood collection is widely practiced to reduce preanalytical variability, yet whether fasting-related differences are clinically meaningful across a broad panel of routine analytes has not been systematically evaluated using clinical data. Objective To evaluate whether fasting duration is associated with routine laboratory test results and whether observed differences exceed established analytical performance specifications (APS). Design, Setting, and Participants Retrospective single-center cross-sectional study using laboratory information system data collected between February 2021 and December 2023 from a single 670-bed secondary-care university hospital in the Seoul metropolitan area, Republic of Korea. All samples were drawn from outpatients at the institution’s central phlebotomy unit. Participants were adult outpatients (≥18 years) with documented fasting duration. Data were analyzed from January 1, 2024, to July 24, 2026. Exposure Fasting duration derived from the time elapsed between the patient’s last meal and blood collection, categorized as less than 8 hours, 8 to 12 hours, and more than 12 hours. Main Outcomes and Measures Adjusted means across fasting groups were estimated using linear mixed-effects models with patient-level random intercepts, adjusting for age, sex, and department. Paired within-person analyses among repeatedly tested patients were performed to minimize between-patient confounding. Differences were compared with the European Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine biological variation–based total allowable error. Postprandial trends within the subgroup fasting less than 8 hours were assessed at 30-minute intervals. Results The final dataset comprised 9 755 547 test results from 101 148 patients across 372 test items. Between-group comparisons identified APS-exceeding differences for 27 analytes. However, only 10 were confirmed in paired within-person analyses, suggesting confounding. Glucose (10.8%), triglycerides (20.1%), γ-glutamyl transferase (14.8%), and lipase (36.4%) were higher with less than 8 hours fasting. No analyte exceeded APS between the 8- to 12-hour and more than 12-hour groups. Within the less than 8-hour subgroup, glucose and lactate decreased significantly with increasing fasting duration, whereas lipid concentrations showed no significant linear trend. Conclusions and Relevance This cross-sectional study found that fasting duration was associated with differences exceeding analytical performance specifications for only a few analytes, mainly glucose, triglycerides, γ-glutamyl transferase, and lipase. No estimable within-person difference between the 8- to 12-hour and more than 12-hour groups exceeded an available APS. These findings support analyte-specific rather than uniform fasting requirements.

item.title: Specialist Referral for Cardiovascular Risk in Patients With Prostate Cancer
item.dc:creator: Darryl P. Leong
Celestia Higano
Cristina Cano Garcia
Vincent Fradet
D. Robert Siemens
Tamim Niazi
Bobby Shayegan
Avirup Guha
item.description:
Authors: Darryl P. Leong, Celestia Higano, Cristina Cano Garcia, Vincent Fradet, D. Robert Siemens, Tamim Niazi, Bobby Shayegan, Avirup Guha, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine; Volume: 186; Issue: 11; Pages: 1381
Abstract: Importance Patients with prostate cancer have a high burden of cardiovascular risk factors, often suboptimally controlled, and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Objective To determine whether the routine referral of patients with prostate cancer to a cardiovascular specialist to implement a systematic risk factor strategy is more likely to reduce adverse cardiovascular outcomes and improve risk factor control than usual care. Design, Settings, and Participants This randomized clinical trial included patients with prostate cancer from 55 sites in 8 countries between 2015 and 2025. Eligible patients were diagnosed with prostate cancer during the past 12 months; had received treatment with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) for the first time within the past 6 months; or planned to start ADT in the next month. Patients taking a statin with a systolic blood pressure of 130 mm Hg or lower were ineligible. Data were analyzed from May 25 to August 7, 2026. Intervention Patients were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive usual care alone or usual care plus routine referral to an internist or cardiologist. The specialists provided a systematic intervention, including a target of systolic blood pressure of 130 mm Hg or lower and a statin medication, irrespective of the patient’s cholesterol levels (even if not usual or guideline-driven practice); encourage smoking cessation; and provide guidance on diet and exercise. Main Outcomes and Measures Hierarchical composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, suboptimal cholesterol (total cholesterol, &amp;gt;155 mg/dL [to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259]) and suboptimal blood pressure (systolic blood pressure, &amp;gt;130 mm Hg) as evaluated by the win ratio. Results The analysis included 2487 patients with prostate cancer (mean [SD] age, 68 [8] years). During median (IQR) follow-up of 5.8 (2.7-8.2) years, the win ratio in favor of the intervention was 1.60 (95% CI, 1.42-1.81), mostly attributable to lower cholesterol in the intervention group (mean difference, 12 mg/dL; 95% CI, 9-15 mg/dL) as a consequence of greater protocol-mandated statin use. Mean (SD) close-out systolic blood pressure values were 131.1 (16.9) mm Hg in the intervention group and 132.9 (18.3) mm Hg in the control group. There was no difference in time to cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or heart failure between groups (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.08; 95% CI, 0.79-1.49). Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, routine referral of patients with prostate cancer to a cardiovascular specialist lead to improved outcomes, specifically through better cholesterol control. However, it is uncertain whether this reduced clinical cardiovascular events. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03127631

item.title: Steatotic Liver Disease Risk Scores to Predict Cirrhosis and Hepatocellular Carcinoma
item.dc:creator: Catherine Mezzacappa
Janet P. Tate
Jessie Torgersen
Melissa Skanderson
Tamar H. Taddei
Amy C. Justice
item.description:
Authors: Catherine Mezzacappa, Janet P. Tate, Jessie Torgersen, Melissa Skanderson, Tamar H. Taddei, Amy C. Justice
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine; Volume: 186; Issue: 11; Pages: 1358
Abstract: Importance Most individuals with steatotic liver disease (SLD) do not develop advanced liver disease. Multiple risk scores for SLD-associated cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have been proposed, but their utility to inform decisions about surveillance for advanced liver disease is unknown. Objective To compare the clinical utility of SLD risk scores for predicting cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with noncirrhotic steatotic liver disease. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used data from the national US Veterans Affairs health system of adults with imaging-confirmed SLD without viral hepatitis or primary liver disease from 2008 and 2020. Nine clinical risk scores were calculated at the time of the first imaging results that demonstrated hepatic steatosis. Individuals were followed up until cirrhosis, HCC, death, or 6 months after last follow-up visit. Data were analyzed between November 1, 2025, and May 11, 2026. Exposures Nine risk scores evaluated for prediction of cirrhosis or HCC within 10 years were: (1) ALBI, albumin-bilirubin; (2) aMAP, age-male-albumin-bilirubin-platelet; (3) APRI, the aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio; (4) BARD, body mass index, age, alanine aminotransferase-to-aspartate aminotransferase ratio, and diabetes; (5) FIB-4, fibrosis-4 index; (6) NFS, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease fibrosis; (7) SAFE, steatosis-associated fibrosis estimator; and 2 additional scores. Main Outcomes and Measures First diagnosis of cirrhosis and first diagnosis of HCC identified using VA and Medicare diagnosis codes and data from the VA Cancer Registry. Cox proportional hazards models were used to calculate time-dependent 10-year probabilities of each outcome predicted by 9 risk scores. Decision curves were generated for each outcome by calculating the net benefit, a weighted measure of true and false positives over a prespecified range of risk thresholds at which a clinician may reasonably recommend intervention. Nine risk scales were used to quantify the risk of cirrhosis or HCC within 10 years. Results The analysis included 853 131 patients (median [IQR] age, 61 [51-68] years; 62 168 females [7.3%] and 790 965 males [92.7%]) whose median (IQR) BMI was 31.3 (27.6-35.5) and 275 898 (32.3%) had diabetes; of these, 33 794 (3.96%) developed cirrhosis and 2978 (0.35%) developed HCC within 10 years. The FIB-4, APRI, and SAFE scores demonstrated the greatest discrimination of cirrhosis risk, while the SAFE, Tate, and FIB-4 scores demonstrated the greatest discrimination of HCC risk. The SAFE score demonstrated the greatest net benefit predicting cirrhosis. A score of 29.5 corresponded to a 10-year cirrhosis risk of 2.5% and yielded a net benefit of 0.019, or 1.9 additional individuals who develop cirrhosis per 100 individuals classified as at-risk patients. At a 0.25% 10-year risk of HCC, the SAFE score had a net benefit of 0.0016 (1.6 additional true positives per 1000 individuals). Conclusions and Relevance The findings of this cohort study show that the SAFE score may inform decisions to repeat screening for cirrhosis in patients with SLD. Clinical risk scores for HCC demonstrated minimal utility to inform HCC screening decisions for patients with noncirrhotic SLD.

Abstract: Importance Routine prostate-specific antigen (PSA) screening in men with limited life expectancy is low-value care, yet US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) PSA testing and biopsy rates have not been benchmarked against non-VA care. Objective To determine whether PSA testing and prostate biopsy rates are associated with likelihood of benefit from screening in VA or fee-for-service (FFS) Medicare primary care. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used national linked VA-Medicare data for fiscal years 2004 to 2023, with up to 20 years of follow up. A 30% random sample of male veterans 65 years or older who were dually enrolled in VA and FFS Medicare Parts A and B were included; men with prior prostate cancer or only Medicare Advantage enrollment were excluded. Exposures Time-varying predominant primary care setting (VA, FFS Medicare, or dual use), assigned from primary care visit distribution across systems over a rolling 36-month window. Main Outcomes and Measures PSA testing and prostate biopsy rates per 1000 person-years. Contemporary incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were estimated with covariate-adjusted Poisson regression and stratified by age and predicted life expectancy. Results Among 1.41 million dually enrolled male veterans (mean [SD] age, 71.3 [7.1] years), 8.67 million person-years were observed. PSA testing declined across settings from 2008 to 2017, with steeper declines in the VA system. From 2018 to 2023, among men 80 years or older, adjusted PSA testing rates were 187.9 vs 267.9 per 1000 person-years in VA primary care vs FFS Medicare (IRR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.69-0.71), and biopsy rates were 3.38 vs 5.05 (IRR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.60-0.75). Among men with fewer than 5 years predicted life expectancy, PSA testing in the VA setting was lower (IRR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.82-0.86). Age- and life expectancy–based differences persisted across sensitivity analyses. In contrast, in the primary analysis, PSA testing in the VA setting was higher among men aged 65 to 69 years (IRR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.09-1.11). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, compared with FFS Medicare, VA primary care was associated with lower PSA testing and biopsy rates among veterans least likely to benefit, suggesting closer alignment of testing intensity with likelihood of benefit.

item.title: Preoperative Medicine for the Internal Medicine Clinician
item.dc:creator: Joan M. Irizarry-Alvarado
Lindee Strizich
Elizabeth Hays
Heather L. Lander
Lily L. Ackermann
Angela Selzer
Moises Auron
Avital Y. O’Glasser
item.description:
Authors: Joan M. Irizarry-Alvarado, Lindee Strizich, Elizabeth Hays, Heather L. Lander, Lily L. Ackermann, Angela Selzer, Moises Auron, Avital Y. O’Glasser
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Internal medicine clinicians are often involved in preoperative evaluation and counseling for their patients, yet explicit training and exposure opportunities in perioperative medicine are limited. Beyond providing clearance for surgery or anesthesiology care, preoperative medical care presents an opportunity for clinicians to use clinical skills, evidence-based medicine, and skilled communication with patients and caregivers to maximize benefit and safety during a planned surgery. This review explores foundations of preoperative medicine to help internal medicine clinicians contribute to safe, high-value, patient-centered preoperative care, including an overview of high-yield resources and professional society guidelines. Observations Delivery of preoperative medical care requires history, physical examination, interpretation of diagnostic test results, and clinical reasoning, supported by a scaffold of published guidelines and evidence. The preoperative examination begins with carefully reviewing the status of known health conditions and current medications in the context of operative risk, which can lead to recommendations for risk reduction and inform the need for further testing. Further, clinicians should also investigate undifferentiated symptoms and other preoperative risk factors that arise during the evaluation, such as exertional dyspnea and examination findings of volume overload. Finally, the preoperative assessment should include communication of individualized risks and benefits of the planned surgery, engaging the patient in shared decision-making around preoperative preparation. A comprehensive preoperative evaluation can not only help patients prepare for surgery but also inform care provided by the surgical and anesthesiology teams during and postoperatively. Conclusions and Relevance Using an evidence-informed, stepwise approach, internal medicine clinicians can have a beneficial impact on the preoperative course for their patients.

item.title: Preoperative Intranasal Oxytocin and Probable Acute Stress Disorder After Traumatic Fracture Surgery
item.dc:creator: Qingqing Huang
Yi Wen
Qin Li
Weiqing Li
Jingzheng Zeng
Qin Shi
Wei Wu
Yinghai Liu
item.description:
Authors: Qingqing Huang, Yi Wen, Qin Li, Weiqing Li, Jingzheng Zeng, Qin Shi, Wei Wu, Yinghai Liu, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Acute stress disorder (ASD) is a common and debilitating psychological sequela following traumatic fracture surgery, adversely affecting recovery and predicting chronic posttraumatic stress disorder. Effective pharmacological prevention strategies are currently lacking. Objective To evaluate the efficacy and safety of a single preoperative dose of intranasal oxytocin for the prevention of screening-positive probable ASD in patients undergoing traumatic fracture surgery. Design, Setting, and Participants This single-center, prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial was conducted at the General Hospital of Western Theater Command in China. From April 2024 to April 2025, adult patients scheduled for traumatic fracture surgery were enrolled and randomized. Interventions Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either receive intranasal oxytocin, 40 IU, or an equivalent volume of intranasal saline placebo 10 minutes before the induction of anesthesia. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of a first screening-positive probable ASD within 3 days postoperatively, defined by a Stanford Acute Stress Reaction Questionnaire (SAS-RQ) score of 40 or higher. Key secondary outcomes included the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC), the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and salivary malondialdehyde, cortisol, and superoxide dismutase levels. Results A total of 328 patients were randomized (164 to the saline group and 164 to the oxytocin group) and included in the intention-to-treat analysis. The median (IQR) age of all participants was 50 (34-57) years; 210 participants (64.0%) were male, and 118 participants (36.0%) were female. The 3-day cumulative incidence of screening-positive probable ASD was 26 of 164 (15.9%) in the oxytocin group vs 50 of 164 (30.5%) in the saline group (risk difference, −14.6 percentage points [pp]; 95% CI, −23.5 to −5.5 pp; risk ratio, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.34-0.79). In the prespecified Cox model, preoperative oxytocin was associated with a lower hazard of a positive screening result during follow-up (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.27-0.75). Exploratory analyses suggested improved psychological outcomes and directionally consistent alterations in stress biomarker trajectories. No serious adverse events were observed. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, preoperative intranasal oxytocin is associated with a lower cumulative incidence of probable ASD after traumatic fracture surgery. These findings suggest that intranasal oxytocin may represent a feasible perioperative preventive strategy; however, these exploratory mechanistic insights and long-term safety profile warrant further investigation. Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2400082612

item.title: Video Decision Support and Advance Care Planning in Older Adults With Advanced Kidney Disease
item.dc:creator: Angelo E. Volandes
Joshua R. Lakin
Yuchiao Chang
Charlotta Lindvall
Lisa M. Quintiliani
Andrew L. Lundquist
Annie Liu
Manjula Kurella Tamura
item.description:
Authors: Angelo E. Volandes, Joshua R. Lakin, Yuchiao Chang, Charlotta Lindvall, Lisa M. Quintiliani, Andrew L. Lundquist, Annie Liu, Manjula Kurella Tamura, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Older adults with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) face consequential decisions about whether to initiate dialysis, yet advance care planning (ACP), the communication that prepares patients for such decisions, is documented infrequently in ambulatory settings. Objective To determine whether a video decision aid about treatment options for advanced CKD, combined with patient-created video declarations, increases ACP documentation among older adults with advanced CKD. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, parallel-group randomized clinical trial was conducted at 12 ambulatory clinics from June 2021 to March 2025, with 12-month follow-up. Participants were adults 65 years or older with advanced CKD. Outcome assessors were masked to group assignment. Data were analyzed in April 2026. Interventions Intervention participants viewed a certified video decision aid depicting 3 treatment options for advanced CKD (hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and conservative kidney management) and then created a video declaration, a recorded statement of goals, values, and treatment preferences in video, audio, or written format, that was sent to their treating clinician. Control participants received usual medical care. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was ACP documentation in the electronic health record within 12 months of enrollment or death, whichever came sooner. Documentation was ascertained by validated natural language processing–assisted human adjudication. Prespecified secondary outcomes included documented discussion of kidney failure treatment options and stated treatment preferences. Results A total of 453 patients were included (228 intervention [50.3%] and 225 control [49.7%]; mean [SD] age, 78.8 [6.4] years; 190 women [41.9%]; 4 American Indian or Alaska Native [1.1%], 8 Asian [1.8%], 38 Black [8.4%], 35 Hispanic or Latino [7.7%], 3 Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander [0.7%], and 375 White [82.8%] individuals). At 12 months, ACP documentation was higher in the intervention group than the control group (56.6% vs 40.0%; rate difference, 16.6%; 95% CI, 7.5%-25.7%; P &amp;lt; .001), as was documented discussion of kidney failure treatment options (46.1% vs 31.6%; rate difference, 14.5%; 95% CI, 5.6%-23.4%; P = .001). After viewing the video, fewer intervention participants than controls at enrollment were undecided about treatment (30 of 227 [13.2%] vs 92 of 223 [41.3%]), and more preferred conservative kidney management (115 of 227 [50.7%] vs 71 of 223 [31.8%]; P &amp;lt; .001 for the overall distribution). Conclusions and Relevance This randomized clinical trial found that, among older adults with advanced CKD, a video decision aid increased ACP documentation and reduced the proportion of patients who were undecided about treatment. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04347629

item.title: Mifepristone Patient Agreement Form and Medication Abortion Knowledge
item.dc:creator: M. Antonia Biggs
Katherine Ehrenreich
Shelly Kaller
Lauren Ralph
Daniel Grossman
item.description:
Authors: M. Antonia Biggs, Katherine Ehrenreich, Shelly Kaller, Lauren Ralph, Daniel Grossman
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance While the US Food and Drug Administration requires medication abortion patients to review and sign a patient agreement form (PAF) under its Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy program, there is limited research examining whether the PAF improves patient knowledge. Objective To determine whether patients are more knowledgeable about medication abortion after reviewing and signing the PAF. Design, Setting, and Participants People receiving mifepristone and misoprostol medications (15 years or older and proficient in English or Spanish) were recruited from 5 facilities in California, Colorado, Illinois, Kansas, and Minnesota (January to October 2025). After receiving standard clinic counseling and the mifepristone medication guide, patients were randomized into 2 study groups and then completed a survey either before (n = 301 control) or after (n = 292 exposed) receiving and signing the PAF. Data were analyzed December 2025 to August 2026. Intervention The control group completed the survey before receiving the PAF and any PAF-related counseling. The exposed group received and signed the PAF and any PAF-related counseling and then completed a knowledge survey. Main Outcomes and Measures Overall medication abortion knowledge (correct response to 12 items regarding when to seek medical care, effectiveness, administration, potential serious risks, and side effects) and responses to each individual knowledge item. Results A total of 593 participants (mean [SD] age, 26.9 [5.8] years; 44 Asian/Pacific Islander [7%], 132 Black [22%], 181 Hispanic [31%], and 159 White [27%] individuals) completed knowledge items (301 control [51%]; 292 exposed [49%]). Across participant characteristics, study groups only differed significantly in reported abortion history. In adjusted analyses, participants answered a mean (95% CI) of 10.37 (10.26-10.48) of 12 knowledge items consistently with the PAF with no study group differences (control: difference, 10.26; exposed: difference, 10.44; adjusted difference, 0.18; 95% CI, −0.04 to 0.39). Nearly everyone knew to contact a “provider” if they “were to have an infection (590 [99%]) or heavy bleeding that soaked through 2 full-size sanitary pads per hour for 2 hours (566 [96%]).” The items with answers that were least often concordant with the PAF included how often the treatment does not work (320 [54%]) and taking misoprostol 24 to 48 hours after mifepristone (458 [77%]). Conclusions and Relevance The randomized clinical trial found that patient knowledge about medication abortion following standard counseling was high. Exposure to the required PAF did not result in a clinically meaningful increase in medication abortion knowledge. The findings raise questions about the PAF requirement from the US Food and Drug Administration, as it does not appear to be useful. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07604675

item.title: Cost-Effectiveness of HCV Screening in Emergency Departments Using DETECT Hep C Trial Results
item.dc:creator: Larsan M. W. Czoty
Sarah Munroe
Emily Stewart
Jason Haukoos
Sarah E. Rowan
Emily Hopkins
Richard E. Rothman
James W. Galbraith
item.description:
Authors: Larsan M. W. Czoty, Sarah Munroe, Emily Stewart, Jason Haukoos, Sarah E. Rowan, Emily Hopkins, Richard E. Rothman, James W. Galbraith, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Nontargeted hepatitis C virus (HCV) screening in emergency departments (EDs) has been demonstrated to identify more patients with HCV than targeted screening. Cost-effectiveness is key to strategy selection; however, the cost-effectiveness of these strategies in EDs remains unknown. Objective To compare clinical outcomes and cost-effectiveness of 2 novel ED-based HCV screening strategies with no ED HCV screening. Design, Setting, and Participants In this economic evaluation study, a cohort of individuals presenting to the ED in the US was simulated with data from the Determining Effective Testing in Emergency Departments and Care Coordination on Treatment Outcomes for Hepatitis C Screening (DETECT Hep C) trial using the Hepatitis C Cost-Effectiveness (HEP-CE) model from a health sector perspective. Using data from EDs at Denver Health Medical Center, Johns Hopkins Hospital, and the University of Mississippi Medical Center, 3 strategies were simulated over a lifetime horizon, including (1) no ED HCV screening, (2) targeted HCV screening, and (3) nontargeted HCV screening. Data were collected from November 2019 to August 2022 and analyzed from December 2021 to July 2026. Exposure HCV screening in the ED. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes were remaining life expectancy, quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs), and costs (2024 US dollars). An annual discount rate of 3% was applied to future costs and benefits when calculating ICERs. An ICER of less than $100 000 per QALY gained was considered cost-effective. Results A simulated cohort with a total of 500 million individuals (mean [SD] age, 46.3 [17.2] years; 264.4 million male [52.88%]) were included in this analysis. Nontargeted HCV screening yielded the best clinical and cost-effectiveness outcomes in the base case cohort, with 65.89% of infections being cured, a discounted cost of $214 465, discounted quality-adjusted life expectancy of 15.8723 QALYs, and an ICER of $12 820 per QALY gained. Compared with nontargeted HCV screening, no ED HCV screening and targeted HCV screening, respectively, had fewer infections cured (65.60% and 65.88%), lower QALYs (15.8717 QALYs and 15.8721 QALYs), and similar discounted costs ($214 467 and $214 462). Absolute benefits appeared narrow because over 90% of those screened did not have HCV; however, benefits were clear among those living with HCV infection. Conclusions and Relevance Results of this economic evaluation study suggest that nontargeted HCV screening was cost-effective when compared with no HCV screening or targeted HCV screening in the ED. Implementing routine nontargeted HCV screening in emergency departments provides good economic value and could be an important pillar of HCV elimination.

item.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Phenobarbital vs Diazepam for Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome
item.dc:creator: Tess Bradley
Megan Feeney
Anica C. Law
Alyssa F. Peterkin
Kathryn L. Fantasia
Allan J. Walkey
Nicholas A. Bosch
item.description:
Authors: Tess Bradley, Megan Feeney, Anica C. Law, Alyssa F. Peterkin, Kathryn L. Fantasia, Allan J. Walkey, Nicholas A. Bosch
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Phenobarbital use for alcohol withdrawal syndrome is increasing, but its effectiveness and safety have largely been compared with lorazepam rather than against more pharmacokinetically similar long-acting, self-tapering benzodiazepines such as diazepam. Objective To emulate a clinical trial comparing patients randomized to phenobarbital vs diazepam for alcohol withdrawal syndrome. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter comparative effectiveness research study analyzed data from the Premier Healthcare Database (October 2022 to August 2024), representing 754 US acute care hospitals. Adult inpatients with a primary diagnosis of alcohol withdrawal syndrome present on admission who initiated phenobarbital or diazepam on the day of hospital admission were included. Exposures Initiation of phenobarbital or diazepam on the day of hospital admission. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary effectiveness outcome was hospital length of stay in days. The primary safety outcome was invasive mechanical ventilation use. Secondary outcomes assessed treatment escalation, complications of severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome, and resource utilization. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation with ensemble machine learning was used to estimate marginal mean differences and risk differences between exposure groups. Results Among 24 643 patients (median [IQR] age, 45 [35-56] years; 18 511 male [75.1%]), 11 919 (48.4%) received phenobarbital and 12 724 (51.6%) received diazepam on the day of admission. There were no differences in hospital length of stay (marginal mean, 4.1 vs 4.3 days; marginal mean difference, −0.21 [95% CI, −0.42 to 0.00] days) or invasive mechanical ventilation use (marginal risk, 3.1% vs 2.7%; marginal risk difference, 0.4% [95% CI, −0.7% to 1.4%]) between initiation of phenobarbital vs diazepam. Secondary outcomes were also not different between phenobarbital and diazepam, except for self-directed discharge, which was more frequent among those initiated on diazepam (marginal risk, 9.5% vs 12.6%; marginal risk difference, −3.1% [95% CI, −4.9% to −1.3%]). Conclusions and Relevance In this multicenter study of patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal syndrome, there were no differences in hospital length of stay or the need for invasive mechanical ventilation between initiation of phenobarbital vs diazepam. These results may suggest near therapeutic equivalence between phenobarbital and long-acting benzodiazepines.

item.title: Communicating Uncertainties About the Benefits and Risks of New Cancer Drugs
item.dc:creator: Avi Cherla
Anita K. Wagner
Steven Woloshin
Courtney Davis
Florence T. Bourgeois
Elias Mossialos
Huseyin Naci
item.description:
Authors: Avi Cherla, Anita K. Wagner, Steven Woloshin, Courtney Davis, Florence T. Bourgeois, Elias Mossialos, Huseyin Naci
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Cancer drugs are frequently approved based on uncertain benefits and risks that are not communicated to patients. Objective To evaluate the effect of communicating uncertainties about the benefits and risks of new cancer drugs on changes in individuals’ hypothetical decisions to take the drug. Design, Setting, and Participants Two randomized clinical trials recruited online a demographically diverse sample of US adults (census matched for age, sex, education, income, and race and ethnicity) from May 9 to July 26, 2025. Intervention Plain-language statements describing uncertainties about drug benefits and risks. Trial 1 randomized participants to 1 of 5 uncertainties: (1) single-arm trial design, (2) unrepresentative population in terms of race and ethnicity, (3) short study duration, (4) surrogate end point, or (5) no noticeable improvement. Trial 2 randomized participants to 1, 2, 3, or 4 uncertainties or to a control group. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome in trial 1 was changes in hypothetical decisions to take a new cancer drug (within-group difference), while in trial 2 the primary outcome was the change in between-group differences in hypothetical decisions (control vs intervention groups). Secondary outcomes included perceived treatment effectiveness, worry associated with taking the drug, and trust in the information and the US Food and Drug Administration. Results A total of 6272 adults were included in the primary analysis (3102 [49.5%] women). In trial 1, learning about uncertainties reduced hypothetical decisions to take the drug by a mean of 10.1 percentage points (pp; 95% CI, −11.7 to −8.5 pp; P &amp;lt; .001). The reduction in hypothetical decisions to take the drug was observed for all uncertainties, including among those in the group that learned that it was unknown whether patients would notice an improvement with the drug (−14.1 pp; 95% CI, −17.9 to −10.4 pp; P &amp;lt; .001) and those who learned that the drug was not studied in patients of similar race or ethnicity (−12.8 pp; 95% CI, −16.4 to −9.2; P &amp;lt; .001). In trial 2, hypothetical decisions to take the drug decreased with each additional uncertainty, demonstrating a dose-dependent effect. Learning about uncertainties reduced perceived effectiveness and trust but did not affect worry. Conclusions and Relevance In 2 randomized clinical trials including a demographically diverse sample of US adults, learning about common uncertainties with a new cancer drug’s benefits and risks reduced hypothetical decisions to take the drug. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifiers: NCT06997185 and NCT07110597

Gary Cutter

item.description:
Authors: Jeffrey R. Curtis, Amy S. Mudano, Gary Cutter, Ted R. Mikuls, Michael D. George, Geoffrey M. Thiele, Mark Law, Kelly Y. Chun, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance The COVID-19 pandemic disproportionately affected patients with autoimmune and rheumatic diseases. Understanding whether certain medications affect the response to a SARS-CoV-2 supplemental dose vaccination is critical for counseling and treating patients receiving targeted immunomodulatory medications. The effect of holding these medications around the time of COVID-19 vaccination on immunogenicity and rheumatic disease outcomes has not been well studied. Objective To assess whether temporarily holding biologic or targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug therapy improves humoral immunogenicity following COVID-19 supplemental dose vaccination in patients with inflammatory arthritis as well as evaluate whether such interruption worsened disease activity. Design, Setting, and Participants The COVID-19 Vaccine Response (COVER) trial was a multicenter randomized clinical pragmatic trial conducted from November 2021 to May 2024 of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and axial spondylarthritis who were receiving care in the Excellence Network in Rheumatology to Innovate Care and High-Impact Research (ENRICH) practice-based network. Data were analyzed from June 2024 to April 2026. Interventions Patients had received a primary messenger RNA COVID-19 vaccine series and were receiving stable immunomodulatory therapy with anti–tumor necrosis factor, anti–interleukin-17, abatacept, and a Janus kinase inhibitor (JAKi). Patients were randomized to continue or hold therapy for 2 weeks following their next COVID-19 supplemental dose administration. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was change in immunoglobulin G levels against the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein from baseline to 6-week follow-up, expressed as the geometric mean fold rise (GMFR). The primary analysis followed an intention-to-treat (ITT) principle, with missing outcomes addressed through multiple imputations. A per-protocol sensitivity analysis was also conducted. Secondary outcomes included disease flares and vaccine-related adverse events. Results Among 840 randomized participants (continue group: 319 female individuals [76%]; mean [SD] age, 60.0 [12.9] years; hold group: 336 female individuals [80%]; mean [SD] age, 59.1 [12.9] years), substantial increases in SARS-CoV-2 spike immunoglobulin G antibody levels were observed across all groups from baseline to the postdose visit. In the primary ITT analysis, the GMFR ratio (hold/continue) was 0.96 (95% CI, 0.36-2.56), indicating no significant difference in humoral immunogenicity between arms. Results were consistent across drug subgroups and drug half-life categories. Holding therapy significantly increased disease flare risk (odds ratio, 2.27; 95% CI, 1.41-3.65), which was most pronounced among those who used JAKi; the Outcome Measures in Rheumatology RA Flare Questionnaire corroborated this perivaccination signal (54 of 256 [21.1%] vs 23 of 253 [9.1%] with ≥10-point worsening; risk difference, 12.0%; 95% CI, 5.9%-18.1%), with full recovery in both arms by 6-week follow-up. Adverse events were comparable between medication arms and were more frequent in the hold group. Conclusions and Relevance This randomized clinical trial found that, among patients with inflammatory arthritis, holding select biologic or JAKi therapies for 2 weeks at the time of supplemental COVID-19 vaccine dose did not significantly enhance humoral immunogenicity and was associated with transient but clinically meaningful disease flare. Routine interruption of these therapies at the time of COVID-19 dose administration is likely not warranted. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05080218

item.description:
Authors: Wei Yu Chua, Luke Xavier Chew, Claire K. M. Chan, Zoe Tong, Lok Pui Ng, Cheng Ean Chee, Dawn Chong, Ravindran Kanesvaran, et al.
Journal: JAMA Internal Medicine
Abstract: Importance Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide. Early detection through screenings has been shown to improve morbidity and mortality. While fecal immunochemical test (FIT) or fecal occult blood test (FOBT) are established cost-effective screening modalities for colorectal cancer, follow-up colonoscopy screening rates remain suboptimal. Objective To evaluate interventions targeting colonoscopy completion and the prevalence of colonoscopy completion after an abnormal FIT/FOBT result. Data Sources MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched from inception to May 9, 2026, and the bibliographies of relevant studies were screened. Study Selection Original studies, published in English, examining nonrandomized interventional studies or randomized clinical trials comparing interventions to improve follow-up colonoscopy after an abnormal FIT/FOBT result were included. Prevalence and risk ratios (RRs) with accompanying 95% CIs for each study were computed, and the results were pooled using a random-effects meta-analysis. Data Extraction and Synthesis This study was conducted in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses ( PRISMA ) reporting guideline. Two authors reviewed each study and extracted the data independently, with discrepancies referred to a third independent author. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes included prevalence and RR of various interventions Results A total of 21 studies involving 19 613 patients (8101 female individuals [41.3%] and 11 512 male individuals [58.7%]; age range, 50-75 years) evaluating interventions to improve colonoscopy completion after an abnormal FIT/FOBT result were included. Patient navigation (RR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.15-1.33; I 2 = 57.1), patient reminders (RR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.04-1.67; I 2 = 89.9), clinician reminders (RR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.12-1.65; I 2 = 94.4), and automated referrals to gastrointestinal consult (RR, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.09-2.60; I 2 = 91.9) were effective in increasing follow-up colonoscopy completion with moderate to high heterogeneity detected within and across intervention types. Sensitivity analyses excluding outliers resulted in low heterogeneity for patient navigation, patient reminders (messaging), and clinician reminders, while moderate heterogeneity remained for automated referrals. Follow-up colonoscopy increased from 4755 of 10 263 in control to 6272 of 9350 after interventions; pooled prevalence estimates were 47.8% and 69.1%, respectively. Conclusions and Relevance In this systematic review and meta-analysis, patient-level and system-level interventions, including patient navigation, patient reminders, and clinician reminders, are associated with increased completion of follow-up colonoscopy after an abnormal FIT/FOBT result. More studies are required to evaluate the efficacy of automated referrals to gastrointestinal consult due to large heterogeneity between studies and to study the incremental effect of each intervention in multicomponent interventions.
